pedagogy.summary: Four-quadrant coordinates extend first-quadrant plotting by carrying each axis through zero into the negatives. The key move is reading a position as an ordered pair — the FIRST coordinate on the x-axis (horizontal), the SECOND on the y-axis (vertical) — and coordinating each sign with a direction. It is best taught by building the plane as two perpendicular number lines the child can already order, teaching the axis-order convention structurally rather than by a first-quadrant rhyme, and working in all four quadrants together rather than bolting negatives on afterwards.
bestPractices: Build the plane as a horizontal and a vertical number line crossing at the origin, so negative coordinates simply inherit the ordering the child already knows from the number line.

Teach the convention structurally: the first coordinate is read on the x-axis, the second on the y-axis; rehearse against the origin (0,0). Treat 'along the corridor, up the stairs' as a first-quadrant crutch ONLY — it breaks down for negatives (to plot (4,-5) you go along then DOWN the stairs), so prioritise 'x-axis first' once negatives appear.
Use points in all four quadrants from the start; have children name the quadrant from the sign pair (+,+), (-,+), (-,-), (+,-) rather than memorising quadrant numbers.
Work both directions — plot from given coordinates AND read coordinates off a plotted point — including negative and fractional values, so fluency is not one-way.

Surface the reversal error deliberately with a compare-correct-and-incorrect task (one child says a point is (8,6), another says (6,8) — who is right and why?), and state the scale of each axis before reading or plotting, especially when grid lines represent 2, 5 or 10.
keyRepresentations: Two perpendicular number lines forming the Cartesian plane, origin labelled
'x-axis first, then y-axis' read against the origin (the 'corridor/stairs' rhyme holds only in the first quadrant)
commonMisconceptions: Reverses the ordered pair, plotting/reading (y, x) — takes the vertical value first (the single most common coordinate error).
Sign/direction error: counts the wrong way for a negative value, landing a point in the wrong quadrant.
Misreads the scale: assumes each grid line is one unit when it is 2, 5 or 10, or reads two differently-scaled axes as if identical.
Over-relies on the 'along the corridor, up the stairs' mnemonic and is stranded when a coordinate is negative (goes 'up the stairs' for a negative y).

learn.summary: Learners plot and read positions in all four quadrants of the Cartesian plane using positive and negative x- and y-values. The core idea: a position is an ordered pair whose FIRST coordinate is read along the horizontal x-axis and whose SECOND is read along the vertical y-axis, with each sign tied to a direction. Build the plane as two perpendicular number lines crossing at the origin so negatives inherit the ordering the child already knows, teach the axis-order convention structurally (not via a first-quadrant rhyme), and work across all four quadrants together rather than adding negatives afterwards.

activities.title: Plot and read on a four-quadrant grid
feedback: If a point lands in the wrong quadrant, mirrored across the diagonal — for example aiming for (-3, 2) but landing where (2, -3) belongs — the pair has been reversed: re-read the first number along the horizontal x-axis, then the second up or down the vertical y-axis.

If the horizontal step is right but a negative y was counted upward (or a negative x the wrong way), rebuild the axis as a number line through zero, count the negative on that line first, then transfer the direction onto the grid.

If a read-back value comes out as half (or a fraction) of the true value, the scale was ignored: ask 'what is one grid line worth on this axis?' and count in those units — a point 3 lines right and 2 lines up on axes rising in 2s is (6, 4), not (3, 2).

When comparing (-3, 2) with (2, -3), if the learner expected a near-identical point, draw attention to the different quadrant as evidence that the order of the numbers matters, because each sign is read on the axis its position assigns.
activities.rationale: Placing a point and seeing where it lands makes the horizontal-then-vertical sequence and the sign-to-direction link concrete, and deliberately contrasting a pair with its reversal targets the most common coordinate error directly. A live grid with on-target feedback, a read-back mode, and a scale control (lines worth 1, 2, 5) makes each sub-skill visible; these interaction examples are optional illustrations, not required mechanisms — equivalent work can be done on squared paper.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils should 'work with coordinates in all four quadrants'.

Misreading the axis scale (e.g. failing to notice the axis goes up in 2s/5s/10s rather than 1s, or that two axes use different scales) is a documented student difficulty when reading coordinates and graphs.

The most common coordinate error is reversing the ordered pair / reading the axes in the wrong order (one pupil says a point is (8,6), another (6,8)); the 'along the corridor, up the stairs' mnemonic works only in the first quadrant and breaks down for negatives (e.g. plotting (4,-5) requires going along then DOWN), so pupils should be taught explicitly that the first coordinate is read on the x-axis and the second on the y-axis, and the reversal is best remediated with a compare-correct-vs-incorrect reasoning task.
learnerActions: Given a target coordinate such as (-3, 2), place a point by first moving horizontally along the x-axis to -3, then vertically along the y-axis to 2, and check whether it lands on target.

Immediately after plotting (-3, 2), plot (2, -3) and compare where the two points land: note that swapping the order of the two numbers (each keeping its own sign) sends the point to a visibly different quadrant.
Switch to reading: a point is shown already marked on the grid, and the learner states its coordinates as (x, y) with correct signs.
Repeat with on-axis points such as (0, 2) and with negative and fractional values so plotting and reading are both rehearsed.
State what one grid line is worth before each plot or read, practising with grids where each line represents 1, then 2, then 5.
activities.intendedInsight: The order of the two numbers and the sign of each carry independent meaning: (-3, 2) and (2, -3) are different points in different quadrants, and the interval each grid line represents must be checked before counting.

activities.title: Name the quadrant from the signs
feedback: If a point is placed in a quadrant whose signs don't match (e.g. a (-,-) point put where (+,-) belongs), check each sign against its axis direction separately.
For (0, 2), reinforce that one coordinate being zero means the point lies exactly on an axis — here the y-axis, 2 above the origin — so it belongs to no quadrant.
activities.rationale: Naming quadrants from the sign pair reinforces the sign-to-direction link structurally and avoids rote memorisation of quadrant numbering, while still realising the curriculum expectation to work across all four quadrants. A reference layout that reveals each quadrant's sign pair and labels the axes ('x first, horizontal'; 'y second, vertical') can support this as a reference, though it does not by itself rehearse plotting or reading.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils should 'work with coordinates in all four quadrants'.
learnerActions: For a given point, state its quadrant by its sign pair: (+,+), (-,+), (-,-), (+,-), rather than recalling an abstract quadrant number.
Rehearse the convention against the origin (0,0): confirm that the first coordinate is read on the horizontal axis and the second on the vertical.
Classify on-axis points such as (0, 2): explain why a point with a zero coordinate sits on an axis and is not inside any quadrant.
activities.intendedInsight: The combination of signs locates which region of the plane a point lies in, and a zero coordinate places a point on an axis rather than inside a quadrant.

activities.title: Compare correct and incorrect readings
feedback: If the learner picks the reversed reading, trace each coordinate back to its axis: the first number is the horizontal position, the second the vertical.
If the learner still relies on 'up the stairs' for a negative y, show that a negative second coordinate means moving DOWN, and restate the axis-first convention that covers every case.
For the prediction, confirm A(3,-2) lands in the fourth quadrant (3 right, 2 down) while A(-2,3) lands in the second (2 left, 3 up) — a different point, reflected across the line y=x.
activities.rationale: A compare-correct-and-incorrect reasoning task is a documented way to remediate the reversal error, and explicitly flagging the corridor/stairs rhyme as first-quadrant-only prevents learners being stranded by negatives.
sourceClaims: The most common coordinate error is reversing the ordered pair / reading the axes in the wrong order (one pupil says a point is (8,6), another (6,8)); the 'along the corridor, up the stairs' mnemonic works only in the first quadrant and breaks down for negatives (e.g. plotting (4,-5) requires going along then DOWN), so pupils should be taught explicitly that the first coordinate is read on the x-axis and the second on the y-axis, and the reversal is best remediated with a compare-correct-vs-incorrect reasoning task.
learnerActions: Consider a dispute about a point plotted 8 units right of the origin and 6 units up: one person says it is (8, 6), another says (6, 8). Decide who is right and explain why, pointing to which number belongs on which axis.

Explain, using a case like plotting (4, -5), why 'along the corridor, up the stairs' is unreliable for negatives — here you go along then DOWN — and why 'read the first coordinate on the x-axis' always holds.
Predict where A(3, -2) and A(-2, 3) each land and justify whether they are the same point or different.
activities.intendedInsight: Reasoning about why a reading is right or wrong fixes the ordered-pair convention more durably than a first-quadrant mnemonic, which fails once the y-coordinate is negative.

activities.title: Accuracy check across all four quadrants
feedback: Expected placements: A in the fourth quadrant (3 right, 2 down); B in the second (4 left, 1 up); C in the third (2 left, 3 down); D on the y-axis, 2 above the origin.
For the sign-change question, B(-4,1) to B(-4,-1) moves straight down by 2 units, keeping the same horizontal position (4 left of the origin).

If A and B land mirrored across the diagonal, the pair was reversed; if a negative lands in an adjacent quadrant, a sign direction was miscounted; if a read-back is a fraction of the true value, the scale was read as units.
activities.rationale: Procedural accuracy across both directions, including negative and on-axis values and non-unit scales, confirms the convention has transferred. Draw-a-path plotting and short read-back responses can score accuracy well, but such checking tasks confirm the skill rather than build the underlying sequence.

Misreading the axis scale (e.g. failing to notice the axis goes up in 2s/5s/10s rather than 1s, or that two axes use different scales) is a documented student difficulty when reading coordinates and graphs.
learnerActions: Plot and label a set of points spanning every quadrant plus an on-axis case, e.g. A(3, -2), B(-4, 1), C(-2, -3), D(0, 2).
Read back the coordinates of points already marked on the grid, including on a non-unit scale (axes rising in 2s).
Describe how a point moves when a coordinate changes sign, e.g. B from (-4, 1) to (-4, -1): which direction and how far.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluency means plotting from coordinates AND reading coordinates from a plotted point reliably, including negative, on-axis, and non-unit-scale cases (fractional values are practised in the first activity).

constraints: Work in all four quadrants from the start rather than adding negatives after first-quadrant practice.

Treat 'along the corridor, up the stairs' as a first-quadrant crutch only; once negatives appear, prioritise 'first coordinate on the x-axis, second on the y-axis', because the rhyme breaks for a negative y (plotting (4,-5) means along then DOWN).
Always state the scale of each axis before reading or plotting, especially where grid lines represent 2, 5 or 10, or where the two axes use different scales.
Rehearse both directions — plot from given coordinates and read coordinates off a plotted point — so fluency is not one-way.

A static labelled plane or reference card can help name quadrants and locate the origin but does not rehearse the act of plotting or reading, where the procedure lives; use it as a reference alongside active plotting.
Recognition-only or read-back-only responses confirm accuracy but do not by themselves build the plotting sequence; pair them with active placement.
Squared paper and drawn axes are a fully adequate substitute for any on-screen grid; the interactive examples are illustrative, not required.
A third spatial dimension is unnecessary for this planar ordered-pair concept and risks adding load without clarifying the two-axis sign-direction link.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of the diagnostic cases: A(3,-2) is 3 right, 2 down (fourth quadrant); reversed to (-2,3) it is 2 left, 3 up (second quadrant), i.e. mirrored across the line y=x — matching the stated reversal error. B(-4,1) to (-4,-1) is a downward move of 2 units with unchanged horizontal position. A point 3 lines right and 2 lines up on axes rising in 2s is (6,4), confirming the halved read-back pattern. Activity 1 feedback now uses only the activity's own (-3,2)/(2,-3) pair to avoid switching example pairs mid-feedback.

The legacy reteach note phrased the fix as 'x is the corridor, count that first, then y up or down the stairs'; this rewrite keeps the corridor/stairs phrasing only as an explicitly first-quadrant crutch and leads with the axis-first convention, to avoid reintroducing the mnemonic's failure for negatives.

A non-preferred alternative (an in-role dialogue) was judged in the source as unable to rehearse the physical placement of points; this is retained only as the narrow objective point that dialogue does not itself exercise the plotting action, not as a universal claim that dialogue cannot teach coordinate reasoning.

The KS3 'work with coordinates in all four quadrants' claim is a curriculum requirement used to ground the all-quadrant scope of activities 1, 2 and 4; no source directly addresses the specific principle of naming quadrants from sign pairs, so that pedagogical choice is carried from the original pedagogy notes rather than from a cited source.

probeDeeper: You plotted A at (3, -2). Where would A(-2, 3) go — the same place or a different one? Show me.
Point D is (0, 2). What is special about where it sits, and why isn't it inside a quadrant?
If I changed B from (-4, 1) to (-4, -1), which way would it move, and how far?
assess.correctAnswer: A sits in the fourth quadrant (3 right, 2 down); B in the second (4 left, 1 up); C in the third (2 left, 3 down); D on the y-axis, 2 above the origin. The read-back point is named as (x, y) with correct signs and read against the '2s' scale (e.g. a point 3 lines right and 2 lines up is (6, 4)).

errorPatterns.pattern: Reverses the ordered pair, plotting (y, x): counts the vertical value first, so A(3,-2) lands where (-2,3) belongs — second quadrant instead of fourth
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reteach the convention against the origin — 'x is the corridor, count that first, then y up or down the stairs' — using the horizontal number line the child already orders.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Watch the order of counting: A and B land in the wrong quadrants, mirrored across the diagonal from where they belong.

errorPatterns.pattern: Sign/direction error for negatives: right-count is correct but counts up instead of down for a negative y (or left/right wrong for negative x), landing the point in the wrong side
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rebuild the axes as two number lines through zero and count the negative on the line first, then transfer that direction onto the grid.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: B(-4,1) or C(-2,-3) lands in an adjacent quadrant; the negative is counted in the positive direction.

errorPatterns.pattern: Misreads the scale: on the read-back, states (3, 2) for a point that is 3 and 2 grid-lines along axes that go up in 2s (true value (6, 4)) — treats each line as one unit
errorPatterns.nextMove: Before reading, ask 'what is one grid line worth on this axis?' Scaffold the count in the correct units; the concept is intact, only the scale was overlooked.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Read-back value is exactly half (or a fraction) of the true value; child ignores the axis interval.

responseLevels.gap: Plots points into wrong quadrants, reverses pairs, or cannot read a marked point back; treats negatives inconsistently and ignores scale.
responseLevels.full: Plots and reads all four points accurately including the on-axis and negative cases, self-checks order and sign, and correctly reads back a point on a non-unit scale — transferring the ordered-pair convention to a new point.
responseLevels.partial: Plots positive and first-quadrant points correctly and reads simple points, but slips on sign/direction for negatives or reads a non-unit scale as units — can place the parts but does not yet coordinate sign with direction reliably across all four quadrants.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is a coordinate grid showing all four quadrants, with each square worth one unit. Plot and label these four points: A(3, -2), B(-4, 1), C(-2, -3), D(0, 2). When you have finished, I will point to a fifth point already marked on the grid (drawn on axes that go up in 2s) and you tell me its coordinates.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who holds the ordered-pair convention and the sign-to-direction link places every point in the correct quadrant on the first attempt. A child who reverses the pair sends A and B into wrong quadrants in a way a correct plot never produces; D(0,2) separates those who treat 0 as a genuine coordinate sitting on the axis from those who drift off it; and the read-back on a non-unit scale exposes anyone assuming one line equals one unit.
